parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ is an odd function.
Given that $f(x)\ge 0$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, find the area bounded by the curve $y=f(x)$ and the $x$-axis, from $x=-\pi$ to $x=\pi$, leaving your answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
A function is odd if $f(-x)=-f(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x) &= 3(-x)-\sin(-x) \\ &= -3x+\sin x \\ &= -(3x-\sin x) \\ &= -f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ $f(x)$ is an odd function.

$f(x)$ is odd, so the graph has rotational symmetry about the origin and the area from $-\pi$ to $0$ equals the area from $0$ to $\pi$.
$$A=2\int_0^{\pi}(3x-\sin x)\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2\left[\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+\cos x\right]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2\left[\left(\dfrac{3\pi^2}{2}+\cos\pi\right)-(0+\cos 0)\right] \\ &= 2\left[\dfrac{3\pi^2}{2}-2\right] \\ &= 3\pi^2-4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{area}=(3\pi^2-4)\text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Writes the integral using symmetry, $2\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}(3x-\sin x)\,dx$, or equivalent merit

The area is the integral of $y$ from $x=2$ to $x=4$ (the curve is above the $x$-axis there).
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_2^4\dfrac{2}{3x}\,dx\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}\Big[\ln x\Big]_2^4\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}(\ln 4-\ln 2)\\&=\dfrac{2}{3}\ln 2\end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Equate the line and the parabola.
$$\begin{aligned}2x&=-4x^2+16x\\0&=-4x^2+14x\\0&=2x(7-2x)\\x&=0\ \text{or}\ x=\dfrac{7}{2}\end{aligned}$$
The root $x=0$ is the origin, so A has
$$x=\dfrac{7}{2}$$

Between the intersection points the parabola is above the line, so the area is the integral of (parabola $-$ line) from $x=0$ to $x=\dfrac{7}{2}$ (part (a)).
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_0^{\frac{7}{2}}\left(-4x^2+16x-2x\right)dx\\&=\left[-\dfrac{4}{3}x^3+7x^2\right]_0^{\frac{7}{2}}\\&=\left(-\dfrac{4}{3}\times\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)^3+7\times\left(\dfrac{7}{2}\right)^2\right)-0\\&=\dfrac{343}{12}\\&\approx 28.583\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}x^3-2x&=x^2\\x^3-x^2-2x&=0\\x(x-2)(x+1)&=0\\x&=-1,\ 0,\ 2\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}A&=\int_{-1}^{0}\left(x^3-2x-x^2\right)dx+\int_0^2\left(x^2-\left(x^3-2x\right)\right)dx\\&=\left[\dfrac{x^4}{4}-x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{0}+\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^4}{4}+x^2\right]_0^2\\&=(0)-\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-1+\dfrac{1}{3}\right)+\left(\dfrac{8}{3}-4+4\right)-(0)\\&=\dfrac{5}{12}+\dfrac{8}{3}\\&=\dfrac{37}{12}\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:

Let $A=\int_{-4}^{-2}f(x)\,dx$, $B=\int_{-2}^{0}g(x)\,dx$ and $C=\int_{2}^{4}\big(g(x)-f(x)\big)\,dx$.

Which of the following expressions equals $\int_{0}^{4}g(x)\,dx$?

solutions.latex:
Let $f$ be even and $g$ be odd. The integrals are signed areas: $A<0$ (region $A$ is below the $x$-axis), $B>0$ (region $B$ is above it), and $C<0$ (on $[2,4]$ the graph of $g$ is below the graph of $f$, so $g(x)-f(x)<0$).

Split the required integral:
$$\displaystyle\int_0^4 g(x)\,dx=\int_0^2 g(x)\,dx+\int_2^4 g(x)\,dx$$
Since $g$ is odd, $\displaystyle\int_0^2 g(x)\,dx=-\int_{-2}^0 g(x)\,dx=-B$.

Since $f$ is even, $\displaystyle\int_2^4 f(x)\,dx=\int_{-4}^{-2} f(x)\,dx=A$, so
$$\displaystyle\int_2^4 g(x)\,dx=\int_2^4 f(x)\,dx+C=A+C$$
$$\displaystyle\int_0^4 g(x)\,dx=A-B+C$$
This is option B.

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$, given $y=(\ln x)^2$.
Hence, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int_{1}^{e}\dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{2x}\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Let $y=u^2$ where $u=\ln x$. By the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dy}{du}=2u \quad\text{and}\quad \dfrac{du}{dx}=\dfrac{1}{x}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= \dfrac{dy}{du}\cdot\dfrac{du}{dx} \\ &= 2u\cdot\dfrac{1}{x} \\ &= \dfrac{2\ln x}{x} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; the single 1-mark row "Correct answer" was written by us.

solutions.latex:
Using $\ln\left(x^2\right)=2\ln x$ and the result of part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^e\dfrac{\ln\left(x^2\right)}{2x}\,dx &= \dfrac{1}{2}\int_1^e\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\Big[(\ln x)^2\Big]_1^e \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[(\ln e)^2-(\ln1)^2\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left[1^2-0^2\right] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes the integrand as $\dfrac{1}{2}\cdot\dfrac{2\ln x}{x}$ and uses part (a), or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ is even.
Hence, or otherwise, find the area bounded by the curve $y=f(x)$ and the $x$-axis in the interval $[-\pi,\pi]$.
can_use: Integrals of odd and even functions

solutions.latex:
Simplify using $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\cos\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} f(x) &= -\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \\ &= \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \\ &= \cos\dfrac{x}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x) &= \cos\left(\dfrac{-x}{2}\right) \\ &= \cos\dfrac{x}{2} \\ &= f(x) \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ f(x)$ is even.

From part (a), $f(x)=\cos\dfrac{x}{2}$, which is $\ge0$ for $-\pi\le x\le\pi$ (since $-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\le\dfrac{x}{2}\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}$), so the area lies above the $x$-axis.

$f$ is even, so the area is symmetrical about the $y$-axis.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx \\ &= 2\int_0^{\pi}\cos\dfrac{x}{2}\,dx \\ &= 2\Big[2\sin\dfrac{x}{2}\Big]_0^{\pi} \\ &= 2\left(2\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2\sin0\right) \\ &= 4\ \text{units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Calculate the area under $y=|2x-4|$ bounded by the $x$–axis over the domain $[0,6]$.

solutions.latex:
The graph of $y=|2x-4|$ meets the $x$-axis at $x=2$, so split the area at $x=2$.

For $0\le x\le 2$, $|2x-4|=4-2x$. For $2\le x\le 6$, $|2x-4|=2x-4$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^2 (4-2x)\,dx+\int_2^6 (2x-4)\,dx \\ &= \Big[4x-x^2\Big]_0^2+\Big[x^2-4x\Big]_2^6 \\ &= 4+12-(-4) \\ &= 20 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

Alternatively, from the graph the area is two triangles:

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 4+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 4\times 8 \\ &= 20 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct set-up (integrals or triangle areas), or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\cos 2x\right) = \cos 2x - 2x\sin 2x$.
Hence, or otherwise, find the value of $\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 2x\sin 2x\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\cos 2x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=-2\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\cos 2x) &= x(-2\sin 2x) + \cos 2x(1)\\ &= -2x\sin 2x + \cos 2x\\ &= \cos 2x - 2x\sin 2x\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrate the result of part (a) over the interval, since integration reverses differentiation.
$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}(\cos 2x - 2x\sin 2x)\,dx = \Big[x\cos 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}$$
Rearranging,
$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} 2x\sin 2x\,dx = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\cos 2x\,dx - \Big[x\cos 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}}$$

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\log_e x-x\right)=\log_e x$
Hence find $\displaystyle\int_1^e \log_e x\,dx$ as an exact value.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule on $x\log_ex$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x\log_ex-x\right)&=\log_ex\times1+x\times\dfrac{1}{x}-1 \\ &=\log_ex+1-1 \\ &=\log_ex \end{aligned}$$

By part (a), a primitive of $\log_ex$ is $x\log_ex-x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^e\log_ex\,dx&=\left[x\log_ex-x\right]_1^e \\ &=(e\log_ee-e)-(1\log_e1-1) \\ &=(e-e)-(0-1) \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Show that $f(x)=x^3-5x+\dfrac{xe^{-x^2}}{1+x^4}$ is an odd function.
Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-5}^{5}\left(x^3-5x+\dfrac{xe^{-x^2}}{1+x^4}\right)dx$.

solutions.latex:
Replace $x$ by $-a$ in $f(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} f(-a) &= (-a)^3-5(-a)+\dfrac{-ae^{-(-a)^2}}{1+(-a)^4} \\ &= -a^3+5a-\dfrac{ae^{-a^2}}{1+a^4} \\ &= -\left(a^3-5a+\dfrac{ae^{-a^2}}{1+a^4}\right) \\ &= -f(a) \end{aligned}$$
Hence $f$ is an odd function.

Since $f$ is odd, the areas either side of the origin cancel.
$$\int_{-5}^{5}f(x)\,dx=0$$

parts.latex: Show that the $x$-coordinate of $A$ is $\ln 4$.
Hence, find the exact area enclosed by the curves and the $y$-axis. Express your answer in the form $\ln a + b$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.

At the intersection the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3e^x}{e^x + 2} &= e^x - 2 \\ 3e^x &= (e^x - 2)(e^x + 2) \\ 3e^x &= e^{2x} - 4 \\ e^{2x} - 3e^x - 4 &= 0 \\ (e^x + 1)(e^x - 4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^x > 0$, $e^x \ne -1$, so $e^x = 4$.
$$\therefore x = \ln 4$$

parts.latex:
Let $f(x)$ be an odd function and $g(x)$ be an even function.

Given that $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are continuous and $k$ is a positive constant,

which of the following is NOT always true?

solutions.latex:
Option A: $g(f(-x))=g(-f(x))=g(f(x))$, which is even, so A is true.

Option B: $f(-2x)+2(-x)=-\big[f(2x)+2x\big]$, which is odd, so the integral is $0$ and B is true.

Option C: $g(-2x)f(-2x)=-g(2x)f(2x)$, which is odd, so the integral is $0$ and C is true.

Option D: $f(g(-x))=f(g(x))$ is even, and the integral of an even function can be zero, so D is not always true.

solutions.latex:

Using the chain rule on the logarithm and then simplifying:
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= \dfrac{1}{x + \sqrt{x^2+1}}\times\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{2}(x^2+1)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\times 2x\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x + \sqrt{x^2+1}}\times\left(1 + \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{x + \sqrt{x^2+1}}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2+1} + x}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2+1}} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
Between $x=-\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and $x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, $\cos 2x \ge \sin x$, so the curve $y=\cos 2x$ is the upper one.
$$\text{Area} = \int_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}(\cos 2x - \sin x)\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} &= \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x + \cos x\right]_{-\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} - \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(-\pi) + \cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right] \\ &= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} + \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 0 - 0 \\ &= \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{4} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Find the area bounded by the curve $y = 3e^{2x}$, the $x$-axis and the lines $x = 1$ and $x = 5$.

Leave your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

solutions.latex:
The area is found by integrating from $x=1$ to $x=5$ (the curve is above the $x$-axis).

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^5 3e^{2x}\,dx &= \dfrac{3}{2}\left[e^{2x}\right]_1^5 \\ &= \dfrac{3}{2}\left(e^{10}-e^{2}\right) \\ &\approx 33028.6 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^3 \dfrac{2\,dx}{5x - 2}$ correct to 2 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The integrand is $\dfrac{2}{5x-2}$. Write it so the numerator is the derivative of $5x-2$.

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^3\dfrac{2}{5x-2}\,dx &= \dfrac{2}{5}\int_1^3\dfrac{5}{5x-2}\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{2}{5}\Big[\ln(5x-2)\Big]_1^3 \\ &= \dfrac{2}{5}\Big[\ln(5(3)-2)-\ln(5(1)-2)\Big] \\ &= \dfrac{2}{5}(\ln 13-\ln 3) \\ &\approx 0.59 \text{ (2 decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes an anti-derivative involving the log function, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Note: do not deduct for incorrect rounding

figures.cap: curves f(x)=sin x and g(x)=1-cos 2x with shaded region between x=0 and pi/2

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where $\sin x = 1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^2 x$, so $\sin x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ in the shaded region.

On $\left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right]$ the curve $f$ is above $g$. On $\left[\dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$ the curve $g$ is above $f$.

$$A = \int_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \big(\sin x - 1 + \cos 2x\big)\,dx + \int_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \big(1 - \cos 2x - \sin x\big)\,dx$$

$$A = \left[-\cos x - x + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{6}} + \left[x - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 2x + \cos x\right]_{\frac{\pi}{6}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}$$

First integral:

$$\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} - \dfrac{\pi}{6} + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - \left(-\cos 0 - 0 + \dfrac{1}{2}\sin 0\right)$$

Second integral:

$$\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\pi + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6} - \dfrac{1}{2}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} + \cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$$

Adding the two integrals:

$$A \approx 0.66 \text{ units}^2 \text{ (2 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Obtains correct primitive, or equivalent merit
Obtains correct definite integral, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:

2845.stem:
The diagram shows the graph of $y=\sin x$ and $y=\sqrt{3}\cos x$, $0\leq x\leq 2\pi$. The graphs intersect at points $A$ and $B$.

\exfigure{1322_q29_1}

figures.cap: graphs of y=sin x and y=sqrt3 cos x with shaded region between A and B

parts.latex: Show that point $A$ has coordinates $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$.
Find the coordinates of point $B$.
Find the shaded area enclosed by the two graphs.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ into both functions.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y &= \sqrt{3}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The same $y$ value is obtained, therefore $A\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$ is a point of intersection of the two functions.

At an intersection, the two functions are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} \sin x &= \sqrt{3}\cos x \\ \tan x &= \sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
Tangent is positive in the first and third quadrants.
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{3},\ \pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3} \\ &= -\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ B\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3},-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)$$

meta.format_note: Source line read $x=\pi/3,\ \pi+\pi/3=\pi/3,\ 4\pi/3$ (repeated value); tidied to $\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{3}=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$.

solutions.latex:
The sine curve is above $y=\sqrt{3}\cos x$ between $A$ and $B$, so the area is
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}\left(\sin x-\sqrt{3}\cos x\right)dx \\ &= \Big[-\cos x-\sqrt{3}\sin x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}} \\ &= \left(-\cos\dfrac{4\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}\sin\dfrac{4\pi}{3}\right)-\left(-\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}-\sqrt{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}+\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}-\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{1}{2}+3\right)-\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}-3\right) \\ &= 4 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive function, or equivalent merit
Shows area is $\displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{4\pi}{3}}(\sin x-\sqrt{3}\cos x)\,dx$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right)=-\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x$.
Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/3}^{\pi/2}\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x\,dx$. Give your answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
Write $\dfrac{1}{\sin x}=(\sin x)^{-1}$ and use the chain rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right) &= \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sin x)^{-1} \\ &= -1\times\cos x\times(\sin x)^{-2} \\ &= -\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}\times\dfrac{1}{\sin x} \\ &= -\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $-\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ is a primitive of $\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\cot x\,\text{cosec}\,x\,dx &= \left[-\dfrac{1}{\sin x}\right]_{\frac{\pi}{3}}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \\ &= -\left[\dfrac{1}{\sin\frac{\pi}{2}}-\dfrac{1}{\sin\frac{\pi}{3}}\right] \\ &= -\left[1-\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\right] \\ &= \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}-1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct primitive function, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Trapezoidal rule with strip width $37.5$ m (the length $150$ m divided into $4$ strips) and the measured widths as shown:

As a percentage of the site:

parts.latex: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^2 \dfrac{6x}{\left(3x^2+1\right)^4}\,dx$ to 3 decimal places

solutions.latex:
Rewrite the integrand as a power and integrate (reverse chain rule):
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^2 6x\left(3x^2+1\right)^{-4}dx &= \left[\dfrac{\left(3x^2+1\right)^{-3}}{-3}\right]_0^2 \\ &= \dfrac{13^{-3}}{-3}-\dfrac{1^{-3}}{-3} \\ &\approx 0.333 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 0.333$$

parts.latex: Find the exact area enclosed between the curve $y=\log_e x$, the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=1$ and $y=3$.

solutions.latex:
The area is between the curve and the $y$-axis, so integrate with respect to $y$. Since $y=\log_e x$, we have $x=e^y$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area} &= \int_1^3 e^y\,dy \\ &= \left[e^y\right]_1^3 \\ &= \left(e^3-e\right) \text{ units}^2 \\ &= e\left(e^2-1\right) \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integral and antiderivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Given that $\displaystyle\int_0^a 5\sin 3x\,dx=\dfrac{10}{3},\ 0\leq a<\pi$, calculate the value of $a$.

solutions.latex:
Integrate, then apply the limits.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^a5\sin3x\,dx&=\left[-\dfrac{5}{3}\cos3x\right]_0^a\\ &=-\dfrac{5}{3}\left[\cos3a-\cos0\right]\end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $\dfrac{10}{3}$:
$$\begin{aligned}-\dfrac{5}{3}\left[\cos3a-1\right]&=\dfrac{10}{3}\\ \cos3a-1&=-2\\ \cos3a&=-1\end{aligned}$$
Since $0\le a<\pi$, we have $0\le3a<3\pi$, so $3a=\pi$.
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$$

2986.stem: Consider the function defined by $f(x)=e^{2x}(1-x)$ where $-3\le x\le 1$

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y = e^{2x}(1-x) with stationary point

parts.latex:
Complete the following table

\extable{1324_q25_t1}
Using the trapezoidal rule with five function values, approximate the area under the curve $f(x)$ for $-3\le x\le 1$.
Differentiate $f(x)=e^{2x}(1-x)$ and show that the function has only one stationary point.
Without further calculus, use the table of values from part (a) to sketch $f(x)=e^{2x}(1-x)$ for $-3\le x\le 1$, and show the stationary point on the curve.
From the diagram, decide whether the approximation underestimates or overestimates the true value of the area under the curve. Give a brief reason.

solutions.latex:
Substitute into $f(x)=e^{2x}(1-x)$.

$$f(-1)=0.27,\quad f(0)=1,\quad f(1)=0$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; single row added.

solutions.latex:
There are five function values, so four strips of width $h=\dfrac{1-(-3)}{4}=1$, at $x=-3,-2,-1,0,1$.

$$\begin{aligned} A &\approx \dfrac{1-(-3)}{2\times 4}\Big[f(-3)+f(1)+2\big(f(-2)+f(-1)+f(0)\big)\Big] \\ &= \dfrac{4}{8}\Big[0.01+0+2(0.05+0.27+1)\Big] \\ &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2.65 \\ &= 1.325 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct trapezoidal rule set-up, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{2x} & v&=1-x \\ u'&=2e^{2x} & v'&=-1 \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= e^{2x}\times(-1)+(1-x)\times 2e^{2x} \\ &= -e^{2x}+2e^{2x}-2xe^{2x} \\ &= e^{2x}(1-2x) \end{aligned}$$

For a stationary point, $f'(x)=0$, so $e^{2x}(1-2x)=0$.

Since $e^{2x}>0$ for all $x$, $1-2x=0$, so $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

When $x=\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$$f\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=e^{1}\left(1-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)=\dfrac{e}{2}$$

The curve has only one stationary point, $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{e}{2}\right)$, or $\left(\dfrac{1}{2},1.36\right)$.
criteria: Sets the derivative to zero and uses $e^{2x}>0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The graphs meet where $f(x)=g(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} x+\sin x&=x \\ \sin x&=0 \\ x&=k\pi,\quad k\in\mathbb{Z} \end{aligned}$$
From the diagram, $A$ is at the first positive solution.

solutions.latex:
Integrate, then substitute the limits.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_{\ln k}^{\ln k^2}\left(1+\dfrac{1}{x}\right)dx &= \Big[x+\ln x\Big]_{\ln k}^{\ln k^2} \\ &= (\ln k^2-\ln k)+\big\{\ln(\ln k^2)-\ln(\ln k)\big\} \\ &= 2\ln k-\ln k+\ln(2\ln k)-\ln(\ln k) \\ &= \ln k+\ln 2+\ln(\ln k)-\ln(\ln k) \\ &= \ln 2k \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $\ln 10$.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln 2k &= \ln 10 \\ 2k &= 10 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=5$$

The diagram shows the graphs of the curves $y=f(x)$ and $y=g(x)$ where $f(x)=e^x$ and $g(x)=6-8e^{-x}$.

figures.cap: graphs of y=e^x and y=6-8e^{-x} with asymptote y=6

parts.latex: State a sequence of dilations, reflections, translations that would transform the graph of the curve $y=f(x)$ into the graph of the curve $y=g(x)$.

Show that the $x$ coordinates ($x_1$ and $x_2$ where $x_1<x_2$) of the points of intersection of the two curves are the solutions of the equation $e^{2x}-6e^x+8=0$ and solve this equation to find the exact values of $x_1$ and $x_2$.
Find in simplest exact form the area of the region enclosed by the two curves.

solutions.latex:
Start from $y=e^x$ and build $y=6-8e^{-x}$ one step at a time.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=e^x \\ y&=8e^x &&(\text{vertical dilation, factor } 8)\\ y&=-8e^x &&(\text{reflection in the } x\text{-axis})\\ y&=-8e^{-x} &&(\text{reflection in the } y\text{-axis})\\ y&=6-8e^{-x} &&(\text{translation up 6 units})\end{aligned}$$
A vertical dilation by a factor 8, then reflections in the $x$ and $y$ axes, followed by a vertical translation upwards by 6 units.
criteria: Identifies one or two correct transformations, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Intermediate lines in the transformation chain were added by us to show the sequence; the source sequence is unchanged.

solutions.latex:
The curves intersect where $e^x=6-8e^{-x}$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^{2x} &= 6e^x-8 &&(\text{multiply by } e^x)\\ e^{2x}-6e^x+8 &= 0 \\ (e^x-2)(e^x-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $e^x=2$ or $e^x=4$.
$$\therefore\ x_1=\ln 2,\quad x_2=\ln 4$$
criteria: Finds the equation and the values of $e^x$, or equivalent merit
Obtains the required equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
On $\ln 2\le x\le\ln 4$ the curve $y=6-8e^{-x}$ is above $y=e^x$, so the area is
$$\displaystyle\int_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4}\left(6-8e^{-x}-e^x\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \Big[6x+8e^{-x}-e^x\Big]_{\ln 2}^{\ln 4} \\ &= 6(\ln 4-\ln 2)+8\left(e^{-\ln 4}-e^{-\ln 2}\right)-\left(e^{\ln 4}-e^{\ln 2}\right) \\ &= 6\ln 2+8\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)-(4-2) \\ &= 6\ln 2-4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the area is } (6\ln 2-4) \text{ square units}$$
criteria: Writes the definite integral and finds the anti-derivative with partial evaluation, or equivalent merit
Writes the definite integral and finds the anti-derivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Solve for $k$ such that $\displaystyle\int_2^k (-3x+1)\,dx = \int_k^6 (-3x+1)\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Evaluate each side using the antiderivative $-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS} &= \left[-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+x\right]_2^k \\ &= -\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k-(-6+2) \\ &= -\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k+4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{RHS} &= \left[-\dfrac{3x^2}{2}+x\right]_k^6 \\ &= (-54+6)-\left(-\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k\right) \\ &= -48+\dfrac{3k^2}{2}-k \end{aligned}$$
Equate the two sides.
$$\begin{aligned} -\dfrac{3k^2}{2}+k+4 &= -48+\dfrac{3k^2}{2}-k \\ 3k^2-2k-52 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} k &= \dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{4+624}}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{2\pm\sqrt{628}}{6} \\ &= \dfrac{1\pm\sqrt{157}}{3} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The area is split at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, where the graphs intersect.
$$A=\displaystyle\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}(1-\cos x)\,dx+\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \Big[x-\sin x\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}+\Big[-\cos x\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\pi} \\ &= \left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-1\right)-(0-0)-(-1-0) \\ &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ units}^2$$

solutions.latex:
On $[b,0]$ the shaded region lies above the $x$-axis ($f(x)>0$), and on $[0,a]$ it lies below it ($f(x)<0$), so the integral over $[0,a]$ is negative and is subtracted:

3254.stem:
The graphs of the functions $y = x^2 - 2x - 1$ and $y = 3 - x^2$ are shown in the diagram below.

\exfigure{1595_q2b_1}

figures.cap: graphs of y=x^2-2x-1 and y=3-x^2

parts.latex: Show that the functions intersect when $x = 2$ and $x = -1$.
Find the exact area bounded by the two curves.

solutions.latex:
The curves meet where the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} x^2 - 2x - 1 &= 3 - x^2 \\ 2x^2 - 2x - 4 &= 0 \\ 2(x^2 - x - 2) &= 0 \\ 2(x-2)(x+1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x = 2$ or $x = -1$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the curves intersect when } x = 2 \text{ and } x = -1$$

meta.format_note: Source also accepts substitution of both values into both equations.

solutions.latex:
The area is the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve between the intersections $x=-1$ and $x=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_{-1}^{2}\left(3 - x^2 - (x^2 - 2x - 1)\right)dx \\ &= \int_{-1}^{2}\left(4 + 2x - 2x^2\right)dx \\ &= \left[4x + x^2 - \dfrac{2x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{2} \\ &= \left(4\times 2 + 2^2 - \dfrac{2\times 2^3}{3}\right) - \left(4\times(-1) + (-1)^2 - \dfrac{2\times(-1)^3}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{20}{3} - \left(-\dfrac{7}{3}\right) \\ &= 9 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct set up of the integral, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source wrote '20/3 + 7/3'; the second bracket evaluates to $-\dfrac{7}{3}$ so subtracting it gives the same total 9. Written that way here.

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: $y=e^{x}-1$, increasing curve through the origin $(0,0)$, with horizontal asymptote $y=-1$ labelled (dashed line), curve approaching it as $x\to-\infty$. The figure id in the source is 1606_q2c_s1 while the sketch_id is 1606_q2(c)_s2.

solutions.latex:
The curve is below the $x$ axis for $-1\le x<0$ and above it for $0<x\le 1$, so the area is split at $x=0$.
$$A=\left|\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{0}(e^{x}-1)\,dx\right|+\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}(e^{x}-1)\,dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\left|\left[e^{x}-x\right]_{-1}^{0}\right|+\left[e^{x}-x\right]_{0}^{1}\\ &=\left|e^{0}-0-\left(e^{-1}+1\right)\right|+(e-1)-e^{0}\\ &=\left|1-\dfrac{1}{e}-1\right|+e-2\\ &=\dfrac{1}{e}+e-2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=e+\dfrac{1}{e}-2 \text{ units}^2$$
criteria: Sets up the integrals with the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 + \ln x$.
Hence, or otherwise, evaluate $\displaystyle\int_1^e \ln x\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\ln x\\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= (x)\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) + (\ln x)(1) \\ &= 1 + \ln x \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), if $y = x\ln x$ then $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1 + \ln x$.

By the fundamental theorem of calculus:

$$\int_1^e (1 + \ln x)\,dx = \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e$$

Split the left side.

$$\int_1^e 1\,dx + \int_1^e \ln x\,dx = \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e$$

$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^e \ln x\,dx &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e - \int_1^e 1\,dx \\ &= \Big[x\ln x\Big]_1^e - \Big[x\Big]_1^e \\ &= (e\ln e - 1\ln 1) - (e - 1) \\ &= e - (e - 1) \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the fundamental theorem of calculus to the result of part (a), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The area under the curve from $0$ to $1$ is found by integrating.

$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,(1 - x)\,dx \\ &= \int_0^1 \left(x^{\frac{1}{2}} - x^{\frac{3}{2}}\right)dx \\ &= \left[\dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{3}{2}} - \dfrac{2}{5}x^{\frac{5}{2}}\right]_0^1 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{2}{3} - \dfrac{2}{5}\right) - (0 - 0) \\ &= \dfrac{4}{15} \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct answer (as a fraction or a decimal; no penalty for omitting units squared)
